title: REG U3·W1 — Income Taxation of Estates & Trusts (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — a taxpayer that is also a conduit

When Jordan Reed dies or sets up a trust for the family, a new fiduciary taxpayer appears: the estate or trust files Form 1041 and pays tax on income it keeps, but income it distributes is taxed instead to the beneficiaries. The entity is part taxpayer, part conduit, and the device that splits the income between the two is distributable net income. This week builds the fiduciary return and that split.

The fiduciary return and who is taxed

An estate or trust computes income much like an individual — gross income less deductions — but with a crucial twist: it claims a distribution deduction for amounts paid or required to be paid to beneficiaries, shifting that income off the entity's return and onto the beneficiary's via a Schedule K-1. Income the entity retains is taxed to the entity; income it distributes is taxed to the beneficiary. This conduit principle prevents a second layer of tax on the same dollars.

Distributable net income (DNI)

DNI is the linchpin. It is the ceiling on both the entity's distribution deduction and the amount taxable to beneficiaries, and it preserves the character of the income (interest stays interest, tax-exempt stays tax-exempt) as it flows through. DNI is roughly taxable income plus the entity's personal exemption and tax-exempt interest, and generally minus capital gains allocated to corpus (principal) — because such gains are taxed to the entity, not distributed. The practical effect: a beneficiary is taxed only up to DNI, no matter how much cash is actually distributed.

The distribution deduction and character flow-through

The distribution deduction equals the lesser of DNI (reduced by tax-exempt income) or the amount actually distributed. The beneficiary then reports that amount, split into its components on the K-1 — so a distribution carrying out $30,000 of DNI that was 80% taxable interest and 20% tax-exempt interest is taxed to the beneficiary in those same proportions. Worked example: a simple trust with $30,000 of taxable interest that is required to distribute all income deducts $30,000, the beneficiary reports $30,000 of interest, and the trust's taxable income nets to roughly zero after its exemption.

Simple versus complex trusts

A simple trust (1) is required to distribute all income currently, (2) makes no charitable contributions, and (3) distributes no corpus. Anything else is a complex trust, which may accumulate income, distribute principal, and give to charity. The personal exemption tracks this: $600 for an estate, $300 for a simple trust, and $100 for a complex trust. Estates also enjoy more flexibility — they may elect a fiscal year and are exempt from estimated taxes for their first two years.

Grantor trusts

If the person who funds a trust keeps too much control, the trust is a grantor trust and is ignored for income-tax purposes — all its income is taxed directly to the grantor, as if the trust did not exist. Retained powers that trigger grantor status include a reversionary interest over 5%, the power to revoke, the power to control beneficial enjoyment, or the right to the trust's income. A revocable living trust — common in estate planning — is the classic grantor trust: fully taxed to the grantor during life.

Compressed brackets, IRD, and the 65-day rule

Trusts and estates face highly compressed brackets, reaching the top marginal rate and the 3.8% net investment income tax at a very low income level — a strong incentive to distribute income to beneficiaries in lower brackets. The 65-day rule helps: a complex trust or estate may elect to treat distributions made within 65 days after year-end as if made on the last day of the prior year. Income in respect of a decedent (IRD) — income the decedent earned but had not received (a final paycheck, an IRA) — is taxed to whoever receives it and does not get the date-of-death basis step-up that other inherited property enjoys.

Putting it together on the family trust

Suppose Reed's family trust earns $50,000 of dividends and $10,000 of tax-exempt municipal interest, allocates a $5,000 capital gain to corpus, and distributes $40,000 to a child. DNI is about $60,000 (the $50,000 dividends plus $10,000 tax-exempt, with the corpus capital gain excluded). The distribution deduction is the lesser of DNI net of tax-exempt ($50,000) or the $40,000 distributed — so $40,000 is deducted by the trust and taxed to the child, carrying the dividend and tax-exempt character proportionally, while the trust pays tax on the retained income and the corpus gain. The conduit has done its job: each dollar is taxed once, to whoever ends up with it.

The tiered distribution system and the separate-share rule

When a complex trust distributes more than its required income, the regulations sort beneficiaries into tiers. First-tier distributions — income the trust is required to distribute — carry out DNI first; second-tier distributions — discretionary amounts and corpus — carry out any remaining DNI, pro rata if they exceed it. This ordering decides exactly how much DNI, and which character of income, lands on each beneficiary's K-1 when there are several. The separate-share rule further requires that, when a single trust or estate has economically distinct shares for different beneficiaries, DNI be computed separately for each share, so one beneficiary is not taxed on income that economically belongs to another.

A charitable wrinkle rounds out the fiduciary deduction picture: unlike an individual's percentage-limited charitable deduction, an estate or complex trust gets an unlimited charitable deduction for amounts paid to charity from gross income pursuant to the governing instrument. Estates also carry unique privileges: an estate may elect a fiscal year (a trust generally must use a calendar year), is exempt from estimated tax payments for its first two taxable years, and can hold income to smooth it across the administration period. These flexibilities, with the tiered rules, make the executor's timing of distributions a genuine lever over who pays the tax and when.

CMA bridge

FAR Unit 2 distinguished an entity's income from its owners'; fiduciary income tax is the same idea for an estate or trust — DNI is the bridge that decides whether the dividend on MBG stock held in Reed's family trust is taxed to the trust or to the child who receives the distribution, with character preserved either way.

Practice and recap

  1. File Form 1041; tax retained income to the entity and distributed income to beneficiaries.
  2. Compute DNI as the ceiling on the distribution deduction and beneficiary income; it preserves character and generally excludes capital gains allocated to corpus.
  3. Classify simple (distribute all income, no charity, no corpus) vs complex trusts; know the $600/$300/$100 exemptions.
  4. Tax grantor-trust income to the grantor; use the 65-day rule and watch IRD (no basis step-up).

Recap: an estate or trust is a conduit — it deducts distributions and shifts that income to beneficiaries, capped at DNI, with character preserved; simple trusts distribute all income (a $300 exemption) while complex trusts may accumulate ($100); a grantor trust's income is taxed to the grantor; and the compressed brackets push fiduciaries to distribute, aided by the 65-day rule.

flashcards.front: Fiduciary return and the conduit principle
flashcards.back: Estates/trusts file Form 1041; retained income is taxed to the entity, distributed income to beneficiaries (via Schedule K-1).
The ceiling on the distribution deduction and on beneficiary income; preserves character and generally excludes capital gains allocated to corpus.
Lesser of DNI (reduced by tax-exempt income) or the amount actually distributed.
Simple: must distribute all income, no charity, no corpus. Complex: may accumulate, distribute principal, or give to charity.
Grantor retains too much control (revocation, beneficial enjoyment, income); income is taxed to the grantor, not the trust.
A complex trust/estate may elect to treat distributions made within 65 days after year-end as made on the last day of the prior year.

flashcards.front: Income in respect of a decedent (IRD)
flashcards.back: Income earned but not received before death; taxed to the recipient and does NOT get a date-of-death basis step-up.

questions.q: Income that an estate or trust distributes to a beneficiary is generally taxed to:
questions.explain: Under the conduit principle, distributed income is taxed to the beneficiary (the entity takes a distribution deduction).

choices: The ceiling on the distribution deduction and beneficiary income
questions.explain: DNI caps both the distribution deduction and the amount taxable to beneficiaries, and it preserves income character.

choices: Distribute all of its income currently and make no charitable gifts or corpus distributions
questions.explain: A simple trust distributes all income currently, makes no charitable contributions, and distributes no corpus.

questions.q: The personal exemption for a simple trust is:
A grantor trust's income is taxed to:
questions.explain: When the grantor retains prohibited powers, the trust is disregarded and its income is taxed to the grantor.

questions.q: The distribution deduction equals the lesser of the amount distributed or:
questions.explain: The deduction is the lesser of the distribution or DNI reduced by tax-exempt income.

questions.q: Income in respect of a decedent (IRD):
choices: Is taxed to the recipient and does not receive a basis step-up
Receives a date-of-death step-up like other inherited property
Is taxed only to the estate
questions.explain: IRD is taxed to whoever receives it and is denied the step-up in basis.
